n: Hebrews opens like a sermon, not a letter. In the past God spoke to Israel’s ancestors many times and in many ways through prophets — visions, dreams, laws, and symbols. Tradition attributes this book to Paul, though the text itself names no author.

f.w: sundry times and in divers manners
f.g: In many portions and in various ways.

n: But now, in these last days, God has spoken through His Son, whom He appointed heir of everything and through whom He created the worlds.

f.w: by whom also he made the worlds

n: The Son radiates God’s glory and is the exact representation of His being. He sustains all things by His powerful word, and after cleansing us from sin He sat down at the Father’s right hand.

f.g: Greek charaktēr — exact imprint, like a stamp on a coin.

f.w: sat down on the right hand

n: He is far greater than the angels, just as the name He inherited — “Son” — is greater than theirs. Some early Jewish Christians apparently gave angels great honor; the author shows Christ is above them.
God never said to any angel, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” or “I will be his Father.” These words from the Psalms and from God’s promise to David point to Christ.

f.w: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee
I will be to him a Father

n: When God brings His Firstborn into the world, He commands all His angels to worship Him.

f.g: Firstborn — highest in rank and birthright.

f.w: let all the angels of God worship him

n: About angels, God says He makes them winds and flames of fire — powerful servants, but servants nonetheless.
But to the Son He says, “Your throne, O God, lasts forever; your royal scepter is a scepter of justice.” The Son is addressed as God and King.
Because the Son loved righteousness and hated evil, God anointed Him with the oil of joy above His companions. “Messiah” and “Christ” both mean “Anointed One.”

f.g: Festive anointing oil — a symbol of joy and royal appointment.

n: Applying Psalm 102 to Christ, the author says the Lord laid earth’s foundation and made the heavens. Latter-day Saints recognize Jehovah of the Old Testament as the premortal Christ.

f.w: laid the foundation of the earth

n: Creation will grow old and pass away like worn clothing, but the Lord remains.
He will roll up the heavens like a cloak and change them like clothes, but He is always the same, and His years never end.
God never told any angel, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.” That place belongs to the Son alone.

f.g: A conquered enemy was symbolically placed under the victor’s feet.

n: Angels are servant spirits sent out to help those who will inherit salvation. Scripture teaches angels still minister to the faithful.
